This register finds 81 Sources financial relationships in which Nvidia has put money, credit or demand behind companies in the AI buildout, and every number on this page links to its source.

Of the amounts that can be confirmed, $30.2 billion Sources is invested and still held, $37.7 billion Sources is committed, and $107.4 billion Sources is contingent on events such as a tenant's default.

More of the summary

$105 billion Sources of the contingent amount is a guaranty of OpenAI's rent that is signed but not yet in force.

Announcements add up to $307.1 billion Sources, which is never counted as exposure; $103.5 billion Sources of it is letters of intent or deals with no disclosed agreement.

Nvidia's own accounts show more than any outsider can name: it paid $58.1 billion Source for equity in the nine months to 25 October 2026, and this register can tie $10.5 billion Sources of that to named deals.

Guaranties of OpenAI's PORTS-Pike leases from SB Energy, capped at $105 billion

Nvidia guarantees OpenAI's lease value at an Ohio campus up to $105 billion once buildings are ready, so it pays exactly when OpenAI cannot. Analysis

FundedNot applicable
CommittedNot applicable
Contingent maximum$105 billionas of 25 October 2026 not yet in force Source (6)
Headline$105 billionas of 17 August 2026 Source (2)

Announced: 17 August 2026 · Signed: 17 August 2026 · Not yet in force · Matures: not disclosed · Last verified: 23 November 2026

Significance82 of 100 why Analysis
What the deal is

On 17 August 2026 Nvidia entered into residual value guaranties with SB Energy, the lessor, covering about 4.25 GW of IT load leased for 20 years to an affiliate of OpenAI Group PBC at the PORTS-Pike campus in Ohio. Nvidia pays only if OpenAI's tenant defaults (insolvency or an uncured monetary default); each guaranty takes effect when its building is ready for service, the first expected in Nvidia's fiscal 2029, and the guaranteed amount declines as OpenAI pays rent. The aggregate cap is $105 billion; the guaranties end on OpenAI reaching a designated credit rating, at lease end, or after 20 years, and OpenAI must reimburse Nvidia. The tenant is VELA I Holdings, LLC, whose parent OpenAI Global, LLC guarantees its obligations by joinder; OpenAI's non-payment is the trigger, so the exposure is recorded against OpenAI, and SB Energy's building subsidiaries are the beneficiaries.

Seniority: Guarantor

Both sides

Result: Partly reconciled

What Nvidia disclosed. 8-K and 10-Q: guaranties capped at $105 billion for about 4.25 GW, nine phases, first effective in fiscal 2029, triggered by tenant default, exposure declines as OpenAI pays, terminates on a satisfactory OpenAI credit rating, OpenAI reimburses Nvidia, option on about 3.8 GW more Source (9). No payments made to date Source. Source (7)

What OpenAI disclosed. OpenAI: secures about 8 GW-IT; 20-year lease; NVIDIA provides credit support for the initial 4.25 IT-GW; rent starts only as completed capacity is delivered Source (4). SB Energy S-1/A: aggregate guaranteed value and remedy cap of $105 billion on the initial 4.25 GW-IT; trigger is tenant insolvency or an uncured monetary default; OpenAI compensates NVIDIA under a separate agreement; 17 leases for about 8.0 GW-IT commencing 2028 to 2032 Source (6). Source (10)

  • optional additional capacity: Nvidia side about 3.8 GW (8-K, 10-Q); 3.75 IT-GW (press release); counterparty side remaining 3.78 GW-IT (SB Energy S-1/A) Source (3)
  • compensation for the guaranty: Nvidia side Site exclusivity for NVIDIA infrastructure given in exchange (10-Q); counterparty side Compensation provided separately by OpenAI under a separate agreement, amount not disclosed (SB Energy) Source (2)
  • if Nvidia declines the option: Nvidia side Not addressed; counterparty side OpenAI must secure a replacement guarantor rated at least A- (SB Energy) Source

Credit read
Wrong-way risk
Specific: exposure grows as the counterparty weakens. Nvidia pays only when OpenAI cannot pay rent, so the exposure is drawn exactly as OpenAI's credit fails; SB Energy states OpenAI is not an investment-grade tenant.
Collateral
No security for Nvidia. The landlord must pursue the tenant parent concurrently Source and Nvidia looks solely to the tenant and tenant parent for recoupment Source. On a trigger Nvidia may assume the tenancy, have the landlord re-let, or sell Source; recovery depends on reletting a campus purpose-built for Nvidia infrastructure. OpenAI's reimbursement and indemnity is an unsecured claim on the defaulted tenant Source (2).
Tenor
Over 10 years: up to 20 years per building from each lease commencement, leases commencing 2028 to 2032; no guaranty is in force before the first building is ready, expected in Nvidia's fiscal 2029.
Cash and undrawn facilities
$4.7 billion (at least), 31 March 2026 Source
GPU collateral
No GPU-backed debt of OpenAI itself found in allowed sources. Compute is mostly contracted from clouds and lessors (Microsoft, AWS, CoreWeave, Oracle, SB Energy).

First order consequences

Analysis

  • If OpenAI's tenant becomes insolvent or misses rent at PORTS-Pike, Nvidia pays SB Energy the shortfall and can recover only from OpenAI's tenant entities under their reimbursement promise. Source (3)
  • If OpenAI Group PBC reaches a credit rating designated in the guaranty, whose level is not disclosed, Nvidia is released, so its exposure depends on OpenAI's credit path. Source
  • Because each guaranty takes effect only when its building is complete, Nvidia's exposure to OpenAI keeps rising through construction even if OpenAI's finances weaken meanwhile (analysis). Source (2)
Second order consequences

Analysis

  • Lender relianceSB Energy says PORTS-Pike's financeability depends in significant part on the Nvidia guaranty, so future project lenders would be underwriting Nvidia's credit as much as OpenAI's; no project debt exists yet. Source (2)
  • Collateral loopOn an OpenAI default Nvidia may assume or re-let the lease, and the campus may host only Nvidia infrastructure, which tests what that capacity is worth without OpenAI. Source (2)
  • ContagionPORTS-Pike makes up most of SB Energy's backlog, so OpenAI's credit drives SB Energy and its controlling shareholder SoftBank as well as Nvidia. Source
Lenders, co-investors and offtakers
  • LandlordSB Energy: Lessor of PORTS-Pike to the OpenAI affiliate under 17 leases of 20 years (about 8.0 GW-IT, commencing 2028 to 2032) and beneficiary of the Nvidia guaranties on the first 4.25 GW-IT. Its data center backlog of about $430 billion is mostly PORTS-Pike. Source (6)
  • Co-investorSoftBank: Controlling shareholder of SB Energy; OpenAI and NVIDIA are also strategic investors in SB Energy. Source
Timeline
  • 17 August 2026: Nvidia signs residual value guaranties with SB Energy for OpenAI's PORTS-Pike leases, capped at $105 billion. Source (2)
  • 17 November 2026: Nvidia reports maximum exposure of $105.0 billion to the SB Energy guarantees and no payments to date. Source (2)
  • 19 November 2026: SB Energy's S-1/A describes the guaranty trigger, remedy cap and OpenAI's non-investment grade status. Source (2)

First order consequences

Analysis

  • If CoreWeave cannot refinance its 2027 maturities, Nvidia's common stake sits behind about $47.5 billion of principal and could lose most of its value. Source (2)

Second order consequences

  • SignalingGalaxy Digital's investor presentation for notes on its Helios campus leased to CoreWeave cites Nvidia's stake of about 11.5% and its capacity order, so an Nvidia sale would remove a support those noteholders were told about. Source (2)
  • ContagionA CoreWeave failure would strand capacity contracted by Microsoft, OpenAI and Meta and remove a buyer that runs only Nvidia GPUs. Source (5)
  • Collateral loopEnforcement on CoreWeave's GPU-backed loans would put used Nvidia GPUs on the market and lower the collateral values other lenders rely on. Source (2)

Significance53 of 100 why Analysis
What the deal is

Under a subscription agreement of 15 September 2026 Nvidia subscribed for $1.0 billion of Nscale's unsecured 2028 Convertible Loan Notes and agreed to a further $1.0 billion, the NVIDIA Sale, settled in notes or non-voting shares and due to close on or around 16 November 2026. The notes accrue interest at 2% rising to 5.5%, mature on 15 June 2028 and convert automatically into non-voting shares at the IPO. They are recorded apart from the preferred shares because they are debt until converted.

Seniority: Unsecured creditor

Both sides

Result: One side only

What Nvidia disclosed. No Nvidia disclosure naming Nscale or these notes found as of 23 November 2026.

What Nscale disclosed. Nscale's S-1/A states $1.0 billion of the notes was subscribed by Nvidia and a further $1.0 billion will be issued to Nvidia in the NVIDIA Sale; the subsequent events note says $2.0 billion of the $3.1 billion programme is with Nvidia Source (3). Source (5)

General: moves with the AI cycle. A fixed loan amount; the exposure does not grow as Nscale weakens, but recovery falls with it, and both move with AI demand.

First order consequences

Analysis

  • If the Nscale IPO fails, Nvidia holds unsecured notes due June 2028 that rank behind GPU-backed lenders, at interest rising to 5.5%. Source (2)
  • If the Nscale IPO completes, Nvidia's notes convert into non-voting shares, so a creditor claim becomes equity priced by the IPO. Source
Second order consequences

Analysis

  • Lender relianceNscale's secured lenders, including Goldman Sachs and JPMorgan, sit above $2 billion of Nvidia notes, so Nvidia money absorbs Nscale losses before theirs (analysis). Source (2)
  • Collateral loopNscale's $24 billion of equipment commitments are largely Nvidia GPUs, so Nvidia's note money helps buy the hardware that secures Nscale's other lenders (analysis). Source (2)
Lenders, co-investors and offtakers
  • LenderGoldman Sachs: A Goldman Sachs affiliate lends under the $1.4 billion senior secured GPU Financing Facility, which ranks ahead of Nvidia's unsecured notes. Source

First order consequences

Analysis

  • Because the exercise price is nominal, Nvidia's Nebius warrant loses value exactly as Nebius shares do, so Nvidia carries full equity risk on the $2 billion. Source
Second order consequences

Analysis

  • Revenue qualityNebius relies on Nvidia for its GPUs, so part of Nvidia's $2 billion may come back as Nvidia revenue; Nebius does not disclose its Nvidia purchases (analysis). Source
  • SignalingNebius raised a term loan, $5.75 billion of convertible notes and a Citi facility after Nvidia invested, so an Nvidia sale would weaken a signal its later lenders may have relied on (analysis). Source (3)
  • ContagionMicrosoft and Meta have contracted Nebius capacity of up to $17.4 billion and $27 billion, so a Nebius funding failure would hit Nvidia's warrant and those customers' capacity together. Source (2)

Significance40 of 100 why Analysis
What the deal is

On 31 March 2026 Nvidia bought 2,000,000 shares of Marvell Series A convertible preferred stock for $2.0 billion in cash, signed and closed the same day. Each share has a $1,000 stated value and converts at about $91.84, into at most 21,778,000 common shares, at Nvidia's option once the HSR waiting period ends. The preferred has no redemption rights and shares pro rata with common stock in a liquidation. Marvell provides custom XPUs and scale-up networking compatible with Nvidia NVLink Fusion.

What Nvidia disclosed. Nvidia's 10-Q for the quarter ended 26 October 2025 reports one facility lease guarantee, maximum gross exposure $860 million, given in exchange for warrants, with $470 million placed in escrow by the partner Source (3). Nvidia does not name the partner. Matching amount, escrow, warrant consideration and quarter identify it as Nscale (analysis). The guarantee is now one of the land, power and shell guarantees totalling $3.5 billion Source. Nvidia never names Nscale, the landlord or the site. Source (4)

What Nscale disclosed. Nscale's S-1/A of 12 November 2026 states Nvidia agreed to guarantee up to $860,340,000 of its obligations under the Ward County lease for the first five years, against a $470.0 million escrow and Series B warrants Source (5). The landlord Ionic Digital's S-1/A states Nscale provided a guarantee from NVIDIA Corporation for the lease Source, a third party confirmation of existence but not Nvidia's side. Source (6)

First order consequences

Analysis

  • If Nscale misses rent on the Ward County lease, Nvidia pays the landlord up to the cap and recovers first from the $470.0 million Nscale escrow. Source (2)
  • A Nscale lease default also makes Nvidia's default warrants exercisable, turning part of a guarantee loss into a larger Nscale stake worth least at that point. Source
Second order consequences

Analysis

  • Lender relianceJPMorgan and Goldman Sachs fund GPUs in Nscale's Ward County building, so Nvidia's lease guarantee keeps their collateral housed even if Nscale stops paying rent (analysis). Source (2)
  • SignalingNvidia's credit let Nscale sign a large Texas lease while it relied on financing not yet committed, so without such guarantees Nscale would need cash deposits instead. Source (3)
  • Lender relianceIonic Digital, the Ward County landlord, has about $1.95 billion of contracted rent over the initial term, and Nvidia's guarantee covers the first five lease years, so Ionic's financing of the site looks to Nvidia's credit before Nscale's (analysis). Source (2)

Significance31 of 100 why Analysis
What the deal is

In September 2025 Nvidia and OpenAI signed a letter of intent under which Nvidia intends to invest up to $100 billion in OpenAI progressively as each gigawatt of Nvidia systems is deployed, alongside OpenAI deploying at least 10 GW. Both sides said details were still to be finalized. No definitive agreement for this structure has been disclosed by either side as of 23 November 2026; in February 2026 Nvidia instead committed equity to OpenAI's funding round, recorded separately.

Seniority: None

Both sides

Result: Partly reconciled

What Nvidia disclosed. Nvidia release: intends to invest up to $100 billion progressively Source. Q3 FY26 10-Q: a letter of intent with an opportunity to invest in OpenAI Source. FY26 10-K (25 February 2026): finalizing an investment and partnership agreement Source. Q1 and Q2 FY27 10-Qs do not name OpenAI as an investee. Source (3)

What OpenAI disclosed. OpenAI release of the same date: NVIDIA intends to invest up to $100 billion progressively Source, details to be finalized Source. OpenAI has published nothing since that converts the letter of intent into a definitive agreement; its February 2026 round release describes a separate $30 billion investment. Source (2)

First order consequences

Analysis

  • The letter of intent ties Nvidia's investment to each gigawatt OpenAI deploys; if OpenAI keeps deploying Nvidia systems without a signed agreement, Nvidia gains the sales without investing (analysis). Source (2)
  • If Nvidia and OpenAI signed the letter's terms, investment released progressively as each gigawatt is deployed would become a commitment tied to OpenAI's own purchases of Nvidia systems (analysis). Source (2)

First order consequences

Analysis

  • SpaceX's AI segment carries billions of dollars of GPU lease payments to Valor, so weaker returns at SpaceXSI would lower the value of Nvidia's SpaceX shares through other income (analysis). Source (3)
  • SpaceX finances AI hardware through Valor equipment leases and a planned Apollo-managed finance lease and is a Vera Rubin customer, so Nvidia's SpaceX stake sits beside sales that depend on SpaceX's leasing capacity. Source (3)
Second order consequences

Analysis

  • Lender relianceAnthropic can cancel SpaceXAI capacity on ninety days notice from early 2027, while SpaceX keeps paying Valor for the GPUs it leased. Source (3)
  • Collateral loopValor and the Apollo-managed lessor own the AI hardware leased to SpaceX, so a faster Nvidia product cycle would cut the collateral value behind SpaceX's leases (analysis). Source (2)
Lenders, co-investors and offtakers
  • LenderValor: Valor leases computing equipment to xAI subsidiaries under three leases with aggregate payments of about $20.2 billion, guaranteed by SpaceX; recorded as failed sale-leaseback debt of $12.9 billion at 30 September 2026. Source (7)
  • LenderApollo: Apollo-managed lessor: binding commitment letter of 24 October 2026 for a GPU master finance lease, about $40 billion of principal, schedules from the first half of 2027, subject to closing. Source (2)
  • OfftakerAnthropic: Anthropic pays SpaceX $1.25 billion per month through May 2029 for about 325,000 NVIDIA GPUs at Colossus (424B4); later expanded to up to $120.5 billion. Source (2)
  • Co-investorTesla: Tesla agreed in January 2026 to invest $2,000 million in xAI Series E, settled in SpaceX Class A shares after the merger. Source

Capacity backstop Definitive Filed Neoclouds Specific wrong-way risk

Nvidia order for CoreWeave's residual unsold capacity

Nvidia must buy the capacity CoreWeave cannot sell through 2032, so its payments rise as demand weakens, until an insolvency ends the order. Analysis

FundedNot disclosed
CommittedNot disclosed
Contingent maximumNot disclosed
Headline$6.3 billionas of 9 September 2025 Source

Announced: 15 September 2025 · Signed: 9 September 2025 · Effective: 9 September 2025 · Matures: 13 April 2032 · Last verified: 23 November 2026

Significance57 of 100 why Analysis
What the deal is

On 9 September 2025 Nvidia placed an order form under its master services agreement with CoreWeave with an initial value of $6.3 billion. CoreWeave sells reserved capacity to its own customers first, and Nvidia is obligated to purchase the residual unsold capacity through 13 April 2032, subject to CoreWeave meeting delivery and availability of service requirements. Either party may terminate on an uncured breach or an insolvency proceeding not dismissed within 90 days.

Seniority: Buyer of last resort

Both sides

Result: One side only

What Nvidia disclosed. No disclosure found as of 23 November 2026. No Nvidia filing or release names CoreWeave's residual capacity order. Nvidia reports only unnamed aggregates: multi-year cloud service agreements of $26 billion at 26 October 2025 Source and, from Q2 FY2027, AI cloud agreements of $36 billion that the AI clouds can stop providing and sell to third parties Source (2). Whether this order sits in either aggregate is not stated.

What CoreWeave disclosed. CoreWeave's 8-K of 15 September 2025, restated in its 424B3 of 26 September 2025, discloses the order form with an initial value of $6.3 billion and NVIDIA's obligation to purchase residual unsold capacity through 13 April 2032. CoreWeave's later 10-Qs and 10-K do not mention the order. Source (8)

  • existence and value: Nvidia side Not named; possibly inside the $26 billion cloud service agreement aggregate at 26 October 2025 (analysis); counterparty side $6.3 billion initial value Source (2)
  • label: Nvidia side Nvidia's own term for the closest category is AI cloud agreements, capacity the clouds can sell to third parties; counterparty side CoreWeave calls it access to residual unsold capacity; neither side uses the word backstop Source (2)
  • remaining performance obligations: Nvidia side Not applicable; counterparty side Not stated whether the order is in RPO. RPO language on committed capacity the Company has the right to resell first appears in the Q3 2025 10-Q, the quarter of the order (analysis) Source (3)
Credit read
Wrong-way risk
Specific: exposure grows as the counterparty weakens. Nvidia pays for whatever reserved capacity CoreWeave fails to sell, so its payments grow as CoreWeave loses customers while it remains solvent. The growth stops at failure: either party may terminate if the other's insolvency proceeding is not dismissed within 90 days, and on termination Nvidia is released from payment for services after termination. Payment also depends on CoreWeave meeting delivery and availability requirements, so a CoreWeave that cannot deliver is not paid. Analysis: US bankruptcy law can limit termination clauses triggered by a filing, so how far the 90 day clause protects Nvidia in a Chapter 11 needs legal review.
Collateral
None. Nvidia receives compute capacity for its payments; no security interest.
Tenor
9 September 2025 to 13 April 2032, about six and a half years.

SPV debt was secured by $22.2 billion of non-current assets at 30 September 2026 Source. DDTL 3.0 tracks collateral GPU by GPU using serial-number documents from NVIDIA or Dell Source. First order consequences

Analysis

  • If CoreWeave's customers take less capacity, Nvidia pays for the unsold remainder, turning a weak quarter at CoreWeave into an expense for Nvidia. Source (2)
  • If a CoreWeave insolvency case runs past 90 days, Nvidia can end the order, so the purchase support disappears when CoreWeave most needs it. Source (2)
  • Delivery delays at CoreWeave reduce what Nvidia must buy, so the order protects demand risk but not construction risk. Source (2)
Second order consequences

Analysis

  • Revenue qualityPayments for CoreWeave's unsold capacity return to Nvidia as GPU orders, so part of Nvidia's reported demand would rest on its own cash (analysis). Source (2)
  • Lender relianceLenders to CoreWeave may treat the Nvidia order as a demand floor, but it terminates on insolvency and is pledged in none of the credit agreements read. Source (3)
  • SignalingNew CoreWeave capacity without an Nvidia purchase floor would be priced on its customers alone, raising CoreWeave's cost of capital (analysis). Source (2)
  • Lender relianceA landlord's noteholders were shown the CoreWeave order as up to $6.3 billion of residual purchases, while the order ends after a 90 day insolvency, so those noteholders rely on support that stops when CoreWeave fails. Source (2)
Lenders, co-investors and offtakers
  • OfftakerOpenAI: Buys reserved CoreWeave capacity ahead of Nvidia's residual purchase; committed up to about $11.9 billion through October 2030 and up to about $6.5 billion through May 2031. Source (2)
  • OfftakerMeta: Initially committed up to about $21 billion through December 2032; its take-up reduces what Nvidia must buy. Source
  • OfftakerMicrosoft: CoreWeave's largest customer in 2025 at 67% of revenue. Source
  • LenderMUFG: Agent or arranger on DDTL 3.0, 4.0 and 5.5; none of these agreements names NVIDIA as a customer. Source (3)
  • LenderJ.P. Morgan: Agent on DDTL 5.5, backed by five redacted customer MSAs that average about three years. Source (3)
  • BondholderGalaxy Digital: Galaxy Digital's presentation for notes secured on a CoreWeave leased campus cites Nvidia's obligation to buy CoreWeave's residual capacity. Source
Timeline
  • 9 September 2025: Nvidia signs an order form with an initial value of $6.3 billion to purchase CoreWeave's residual unsold capacity through 13 April 2032. Source (3)
  • 15 September 2025: CoreWeave files an 8-K disclosing the Nvidia order and its insolvency termination terms. Source (2)
  • 31 December 2025: CoreWeave amends DDTL 3.0 for delivery delays, cutting minimum liquidity to $100 million and postponing the coverage test. Source (4)
  • 31 March 2026: CoreWeave signs the $8.5 billion non-recourse DDTL 4.0 with MUFG as agent; no Nvidia agreement is pledged. Source (2)
  • 18 May 2026: CoreWeave signs the $3.1 billion DDTL 5.0 with Morgan Stanley as agent, backed by two non-investment grade customers. Source (2)
  • 10 August 2026: CoreWeave signs the $2.6 billion DDTL 5.5 with JPMorgan as agent, backed by five redacted customer contracts. Source (2)

Significance50 of 100 why Analysis
What the deal is

Under a Master Cloud Services Agreement and Order Form 1 dated 8 June 2026, SharonAI reserves GPU capacity for Nvidia for six years, delivered in five phases. Nvidia will have little or no use of the capacity unless SharonAI cannot sell it to third parties; minimum revenue provisions apply, subject to third-party utilisation, and Nvidia earns a share of cloud revenue on capacity sold. SharonAI describes the structure as a revenue-sharing and credit-support model.

CommittedNot disclosed

Announced: 28 June 2026 · Matures: not disclosed · Last verified: 23 November 2026

Significance55 of 100 why Analysis
What the deal is

Firmus announced a strategic compute partnership with NVIDIA running through 2034, anchored by a 360 MW NVIDIA DSX campus in Batam, Indonesia, covering up to 170,000 NVIDIA accelerators. Firmus procures NVIDIA infrastructure through a revenue-sharing and credit-support model: NVIDIA earns product revenue plus a share of cloud revenue on the supported capacity. Nvidia's own blog names Firmus as one of the first partners in this model. Neither side discloses the size or trigger of the credit support.

Seniority: Buyer of last resort

Both sides

Result: Partly reconciled

What Nvidia disclosed. Nvidia's blog of 1 July 2026 describes a revenue-sharing and credit-support model for AI clouds and names Firmus and its Batam campus (360 MW, up to 170,000 GPUs). Nvidia's 10-Q for the quarter ended 26 July 2026 reports AI cloud agreements in aggregate ($36 billion) without naming partners. Source (5)

What Firmus disclosed. Firmus release of 28 June 2026: partnership through 2034, revenue-sharing and credit-support model, up to 170,000 accelerators, expected US$25 to 30 billion from committed offtake over six years. Source (5)

  • term: Nvidia side Not stated in the Nvidia blog; counterparty side Through 2034 Source
  • amount: Nvidia side Included, if at all, only in the unattributed AI cloud agreements aggregate; counterparty side Not stated; Firmus gives expected customer offtake, not Nvidia's commitment Source (2)

What the deal is

Alongside the January 2026 share purchase, Nvidia and CoreWeave announced a collaboration framework to accelerate CoreWeave's buildout of more than 5 gigawatts of AI factories by 2030. The companies intend to use Nvidia's financial strength to speed CoreWeave's procurement of land, power and shell. CoreWeave states it is subject to future agreements or order forms; no amount, guarantee or financing has been disclosed.

Seniority: None

Both sides

Result: Partly reconciled

  • Without signed Nvidia support, CoreWeave must finance its site buildout on its own high-yield credit. Source (2)

Circular flows

Where Nvidia money goes out and comes back as demand for Nvidia systems. No loop has a disclosed dollar value on its return leg, so no circularity ratio can be computed.

PORTS-Pike: Nvidia stands behind OpenAI's rent on a campus that must run Nvidia systems

Closed loop · Analysis

Nvidia buys SB Energy stock and guarantees the landlord against an OpenAI rent default. Once buildings are ready, OpenAI will pay rent to SB Energy, and the site must deploy only Nvidia reference architecture. No rent, guaranty or system purchase is in effect yet.

  1. Out: Nvidia to SB Energy. Prepaid forward for SB Energy Class N stock, funded; a further placement at the IPO is committed Source (2)$1.5 billion funded
  2. Out: Nvidia to SB Energy. Residual value guaranties to the PORTS building landlords for leases of about 4.25 GW-IT to an OpenAI affiliate; paid only on tenant insolvency or uncured monetary default; not in force until a building is ready for service, the first expected in Nvidia's fiscal 2029 Source (6)$105 billion cap
  3. Onward: OpenAI to SB Energy. Rent under 17 twenty-year leases of about 8.0 GW-IT, commencing 2028 to 2032; rent total not disclosed Source (2)Amount: not disclosed
  4. Back: OpenAI to Nvidia. Compensation to Nvidia for the guaranty under a separate letter agreement; amount not disclosed Source (2)Amount: not disclosed
  5. Back: OpenAI to Nvidia. The premises must exclusively deploy Nvidia reference architecture for at least 20 years; no purchase value disclosed Source (2)Amount: exclusivity, no value

Closing leg is sourced as a contractual obligation (site exclusivity), not as a dollar amount. A ratio needs OpenAI's or SB Energy's disclosed spending on Nvidia systems for PORTS-Pike; neither side discloses it, so the ratio is not computable. The guaranty is contingent, not paid (no payments to date, Source).

OpenAI: Nvidia equity in, Nvidia-based compute contracts out

Closed loop · Analysis

Nvidia commits equity to OpenAI's funding round, and OpenAI pairs the investment with dedicated Vera Rubin capacity and contracts with clouds that run Nvidia GPUs. CoreWeave, one of those clouds, runs only Nvidia GPUs, so part of the round can return to Nvidia as hardware sales; no amount is disclosed.

  1. Out: Nvidia to OpenAI. Investment in OpenAI's 2026 round, disclosed by OpenAI; funded amount and schedule not disclosed Source (3)$30 billion committed
  2. Back: OpenAI to Nvidia. 3 GW of dedicated inference and 2 GW of training on Vera Rubin, paired with the investment; no dollar value SourceAmount: capacity, no value
  3. Onward: OpenAI to CoreWeave. OpenAI master services agreement with CoreWeave of March 2025, signed before the 2026 round, up to about this amount through October 2030 Source$11.9 billion up to (contract signed March 2025, before the round)
  4. Back: CoreWeave to Nvidia. All GPUs in CoreWeave's fleet are Nvidia GPUs; Nvidia was 17% of CoreWeave's 2025 supplier purchases, dollar value not stated Source (2)Amount: share of purchases, no value

Nvidia's side is sourced only from OpenAI (Nvidia does not name the investment). OpenAI's spending on Nvidia hardware is not disclosed in dollars; the Vera Rubin capacity has no value, and Microsoft's Azure contract does not name Nvidia hardware as use of proceeds, so it does not count. Ratio not computable. OpenAI's $250 billion Azure contract ( Source, 29 October 2025) predates the February 2026 round, so it is no longer drawn as a leg of this loop.

Anthropic: Nvidia stock purchase, then Nvidia GPU capacity from Nvidia-backed clouds

Closed loop · Analysis

Nvidia buys Anthropic stock in the IPO placement, and Anthropic has agreed to spend on Nvidia GPU compute at SpaceX, Nscale and Lambda. SpaceX and Nscale are Nvidia customers or buy Nvidia GPUs; Lambda's purchases are not on file. Nvidia also holds equity in SpaceX, Nscale and Lambda, so money leaves Nvidia once and can return through several paths.

  1. Out: Nvidia to Anthropic. 120,481,927 Class N shares bought in the IPO concurrent private placement, closed 20 November 2026 Source (2)$10 billion funded
  2. Onward: Anthropic to SpaceX. SpaceXAI arrangements for Nvidia GPU compute into 2029, cancellable on 90 days notice after initial periods Source (2)$120.5 billion up to (contract)
  3. Onward: Anthropic to Nscale. Nscale GPU services agreements for Nvidia GPU compute into 2033; Nscale has no binding financing yet Source (2)$44.6 billion up to (contract)
  4. Onward: Anthropic to Lambda. Lambda agreements for Nvidia GPU compute into 2034; the August 2026 agreement is terminable Source (2)$41.3 billion contract value
  5. Back: SpaceX to Nvidia. SpaceXAI deploys Nvidia Vera CPUs and Vera Rubin systems; no value disclosed Source (2)Amount: customer, no value
  6. Back: Nscale to Nvidia. Nvidia is Nscale's primary GPU manufacturer, bought through OEMs; no value tied to the Anthropic contract Source (2)Amount: supplier, no value

Nvidia's funded side is sourced (Anthropic 424B4). The return side is sourced only as supplier relationships without dollar values; none of the three clouds discloses Nvidia hardware bought for Anthropic. Ratio not computable. Nvidia's portion of Anthropic's Series G is not disclosed (Anthropic: agreement to invest up to $10 billion (November 2025), partly funded in Series G).

CoreWeave: shareholder, supplier, renter and buyer of unsold capacity

Closed loop · Analysis

Nvidia owns CoreWeave stock, is the maker of every GPU in its fleet, rents compute from it and has agreed to buy capacity CoreWeave cannot sell to its own customers. Money flows to CoreWeave as equity and rent and flows back to Nvidia as GPU purchases, whose dollar value CoreWeave does not disclose.

  1. Out: Nvidia to CoreWeave. 22,935,780 Class A shares at $87.20, January 2026 (earlier holding cost not disclosed) Source (2)$2 billion funded
  2. Out: Nvidia to CoreWeave. Payments under the 2023 master services agreement: about $320 million to end 2024, $326.3 million in 2025, $59.6 million in Q1 2026 (sum $705.9 million, analysis) Source (3)Amount: paid, components only
  3. Out: Nvidia to CoreWeave. Order to buy CoreWeave's residual unsold capacity through 13 April 2032, initial value of the order form, not a cap; ends after a 90 day insolvency Source (3)$6.3 billion initial value (headline)
  4. Back: CoreWeave to Nvidia. All GPUs are Nvidia GPUs; Nvidia was 17% of 2025 supplier purchases; dollar value not disclosed Source (2)Amount: share of purchases, no value

Round trip can be shown side by side only partly: Nvidia's rent paid is sourced ($705.9 million in components) but CoreWeave gives Nvidia's share of purchases (17%) without a dollar figure, and its $7.4 billion of OEM financing names no OEM Source. Ratio not computable without CoreWeave's dollar purchases from Nvidia.

Nscale: shareholder, noteholder, lease guarantor and customer

Closed loop · Analysis

Nvidia holds Nscale preferred shares and convertible notes, guarantees its Ward County lease and rents reserved GPU capacity from it. Nscale buys Nvidia GPUs through OEMs to build that capacity, so Nvidia's cash and credit can come back as hardware demand; no amount is disclosed.

  1. Out: Nvidia to Nscale. Series B, SAFE converted to Series C-3, and Series C-4 preferred shares Source (3)$1.18 billion funded
  2. Out: Nvidia to Nscale. 2028 convertible loan notes subscribed; a further $1.0 billion NVIDIA Sale is committed, closing not confirmed Source (2)$1 billion funded
  3. Out: Nvidia to Nscale. Guarantee of Nscale's Ward County, Texas lease for its first five years, against a $470.0 million escrow and warrants Source (3)$860.3 million cap
  4. Out: Nvidia to Nscale. NVIDIA master cloud services agreement for reserved GPU cluster capacity in Iceland, the UK and Norway Source (2)$1.2 billion contract value
  5. Back: Nscale to Nvidia. Nvidia is the primary manufacturer of Nscale's GPUs, bought through third-party OEMs; no dollar value Source (2)Amount: supplier, no value

Nvidia's side is sourced from Nscale's S-1/A only (Nvidia names neither the stake nor the notes; the guarantee appears anonymously at $860 million). Nscale's purchases go through OEMs, which count only where a filing names Nvidia hardware; the S-1/A names Nvidia as primary GPU manufacturer but gives no dollar value. Ratio not computable.

IREN: Nvidia cloud contract and share rights booked into GPU cost

Closed loop · Analysis

Nvidia signed a five-year cloud services contract with IREN and received a right to buy IREN shares. IREN buys GPUs from Nvidia and booked the value of Nvidia's share rights as part of the cost of those GPUs, so part of the GPU price is paid in IREN equity options.

  1. Out: Nvidia to IREN. Five-year cloud services contract under which Nvidia is IREN's customer Source (3)$3.4 billion contract value
  2. Back: IREN to Nvidia. Right for Nvidia to buy up to 30 million IREN shares at $70, vesting with delivery of up to 600,000 GPUs; not exercised as reported Source (3)$2.1 billion headline (option, up to)
  3. Back: IREN to Nvidia. GPUs acquired from Nvidia; the rights' fair value of about $793.4 million was capitalised into their cost (dollar value of the GPU purchase not stated) Source (2)Amount: purchase, no value

Nvidia's payments under the contract are not disclosed (only total contract value). IREN's GPU purchases from Nvidia have no stated dollar total; the $793.4 million fair value is a component of cost, not the purchase price. Ratio not computable; a round trip needs IREN's disclosed Nvidia purchases and Nvidia's payments in the same window.

NAVER: Nvidia equity tied to a Brookfield GPU vehicle that NAVER guarantees

Open at the closing leg · Analysis

Nvidia's investment in NAVER was conditional on NAVER securing project financing, which it met with a Brookfield vehicle that will buy GPUs and data centers. NAVER guarantees its cloud unit's usage fees to the vehicle, and the expansion is an Nvidia DSX AI factory, so Nvidia's equity helped trigger financing for a site Nvidia describes as its own AI factory design; no source says whose GPUs the vehicle buys.

  1. Out: Nvidia to NAVER. Private placement of new NAVER shares; precondition met 27 October 2026, closing pending Source (3)$1 billion committed
  2. Onward: Brookfield to NAVER. Brookfield vehicle to invest in GPUs and data centers and provide computing power to NAVER Cloud; GPU vendor not named in the NAVER release Source$9 billion up to (vehicle investment; vendor not named)
  3. Onward: NAVER to Brookfield. NAVER guarantees NAVER Cloud's usage fees to the vehicle for up to eight years SourceAmount: not disclosed
  4. Out: Nvidia to Brookfield. Nvidia is a strategic limited partner in Brookfield's AI infrastructure fund; amount not disclosed; link to the NAVER vehicle not stated Source (2)Amount: not disclosed

Open at the closing leg: the Nvidia release describes the site as an Nvidia DSX AI factory, but no allowed source states that the Brookfield vehicle's GPUs are bought from Nvidia or their value. Needs the vehicle's purchase terms. Nvidia's $1 billion is not yet funded.

SharonAI: Nvidia minimum revenue on capacity SharonAI buys Nvidia hardware to build

Closed loop · Analysis

Nvidia agreed to pay SharonAI minimum revenue for reserved capacity it uses only when third parties do not buy it, with a revenue share. SharonAI committed to buy computing hardware for that capacity, so Nvidia's promise supports demand for its own GPUs.

  1. Out: Nvidia to SharonAI. Master Cloud Services Agreement: minimum revenue subject to third-party utilisation; the 8-K says up to $4.88 billion, the 10-Q says no fixed aggregate value Source (4)$4.88 billion headline (up to)
  2. Back: SharonAI to Nvidia. Commitment of about $4 billion for hardware and infrastructure in connection with the Nvidia agreement; Nvidia GPUs named in the collateral note, vendor split not stated Source (2)Amount: commitment, vendor split not stated

Both sides are sourced only by SharonAI. Nvidia's committed amount and payments are not disclosed (headline only). The hardware commitment is about $4 billion but the share paid to Nvidia is not stated, so the ratio is not computable. SharonAI says it must keep access to additional financing Source.

Firmus: Nvidia equity and credit support for an Nvidia-only campus

Closed loop · Analysis

Nvidia is named in three Firmus equity rounds, one of them subject to closing, and gives the Batam campus revenue-sharing and credit support. The campus is a dedicated Nvidia DSX AI factory, so Nvidia's equity and support can return as system sales; no amount is disclosed.

  1. Out: Nvidia to Firmus. Participation in the $505 million round (subject to closing) and follow-on in the $2 billion round; Nvidia amounts not disclosed Source (2)Amount: not disclosed
  2. Out: Nvidia to Firmus. Revenue-sharing and credit-support model for the Batam campus through 2034; size, form and trigger not disclosed Source (2)Amount: not disclosed
  3. Back: Firmus to Nvidia. Dedicated 360 MW Nvidia DSX AI factory campus, up to 170,000 accelerators; no value SourceAmount: capacity, no value

No dollar amount on either side is disclosed. Needs Nvidia's investment amounts and Firmus's purchases from Nvidia. One news report, unconfirmed, says Firmus withdrew its listing application Source.

Nebius: Nvidia warrant money in, sole-supplier GPU purchases back

Closed loop · Analysis

Nvidia paid for a pre-funded warrant over Nebius shares, and Nebius says it relies on Nvidia for the GPU chips it uses. The loop closes through hardware purchases, but no Nvidia rental, backstop or guarantee was found.

  1. Out: Nvidia to Nebius. Pre-funded warrant over 21,065,936 Class A shares Source (2)$2 billion funded
  2. Back: Nebius to Nvidia. Nebius relies on Nvidia for the GPU chips it uses; purchase value not disclosed SourceAmount: supplier, no value

Nvidia's side is reconciled on both sides. Nebius does not disclose its Nvidia purchases, so the ratio is not computable.

SpaceX: Nvidia holds SpaceX shares partly from xAI stakes, and SpaceX buys Nvidia systems

Closed loop · Analysis

Nvidia holds SpaceX shares that came at least partly from xAI stakes when SpaceX acquired xAI; their cost is not disclosed. SpaceX's AI unit is an Nvidia customer, finances its GPUs through lessors with no Nvidia money found, and sells the capacity to Anthropic, another Nvidia investee.

  1. Out: Nvidia to SpaceX. SpaceX Class A shares held by Nvidia, at least partly from xAI holdings including the Series E; cost not disclosed Source (3)Amount: cost not disclosed; 13F value $19.7 billion at 30 September 2026
  2. Onward: Valor to SpaceX. Valor leases computing equipment to xAI subsidiaries; recorded by SpaceX as failed sale-leaseback debt Source (2)$12.9 billion debt recorded
  3. Onward: Anthropic to SpaceX. Anthropic pays SpaceX $1.25 billion per month through May 2029 for about 325,000 Nvidia GPUs at Colossus SourceAmount: monthly rate
  4. Back: SpaceX to Nvidia. SpaceXAI deploys Nvidia Vera CPUs and Vera Rubin systems; no value Source (2)Amount: customer, no value

Nvidia's money in is not sourced as a cost (only market value). SpaceX's Nvidia purchases have no value. Seed A3's Nvidia stake in a GPU vehicle is unconfirmed (single Bloomberg report). Ratio not computable.

Blue legs are money out from Nvidia, ochre legs are purchases or payments back to Nvidia, pink legs are rent, gray legs run between other companies. Each leg says Out, Back or Onward in words.

Stress

These illustrate how losses would travel, not forecasts.

Defaults are illustrative, not anchored to an observed move. Choosing a scenario rings the companies it touches on the map; the map legend has a control to clear the rings.

Who else guarantees AI capacity

Nvidia is the largest underwriter of AI capacity, but not the only one. Google, Broadcom and AMD stand behind demand for their own chips with the same tools, and Meta stands behind capacity it will use. Each figure below is that company's largest disclosed amount, so they cannot be added across companies. Analysis

ProviderLargest disclosed figureWhat it stands behind
Nvidia$118 billion SourceGuarantees of leases and other obligations, mostly OpenAI's rent in Ohio; $105 billion is signed but not yet in force
Broadcomabout $161.2 billion Source
Broadcom leases its own TPU based AI hardware to Anthropic's lease subsidiaries instead of selling it, on five year finance leases with rent of about $161.2 billion excluding interest, payable from ready for service.

Anthropic posted restricted cash for Broadcom's benefit and may have to post more.

4 arrangements: Backstop, Credit support, Residual value guarantee, Vendor financing Sources (3)
Anthropicabout $121.3 billion Source
Anthropic committed to spend at least about $121.3 billion with Google between April 2026 and July 2033 regardless of actual usage, paying any shortfall as a true-up.

It is non-cancelable except for Google's uncured material breach. The capacity is Google TPUs, not Nvidia.

7 arrangements: Contract lenders rely on, Credit support, Guarantee, Minimum commitment, Parent guarantee Sources (2)
Google$75.7 billion Source
Alphabet reports $75.7 billion of backstop obligations on data center lease payments and related energy costs at 30 September 2026.

Of that, $48.0 billion is executed with third-party data center providers; $27.7 billion is an obligation to put future backstops in place, including $10.0 billion for Crux AI. The named Fluidstack and Anthropic backstops sit inside this total.

8 arrangements: Backstop, Credit support, Residual value guarantee Sources (5)
Meta$28.1 billion Source
Meta sold 80% of its Louisiana data center campus to a venture owned by a Blue Owl fund affiliate and leases the campus back from 2029 on four-year terms renewable to 20 years.

If Meta ends or does not renew a lease, it pays any shortfall between the property's fair value and a guaranteed threshold. The venture is off Meta's balance sheet.

3 arrangements: Backstop, Residual value guarantee Sources (11)
SpaceX$20.2 billion Source (9)
Three leases under which an xAI subsidiary leases computing equipment from Valor, with aggregate payments of $6,986 million, $6,633 million and $6,587 million, are guaranteed by SpaceX or a subsidiary.

SpaceX accounts for them as a failed sale-leaseback, with $12,897 million of debt at 30 September 2026. The lessee paid $885 million in 2025 and $1,917 million from January to April 2026.

1 arrangement: Lease guarantee Sources (9)
Amazonup to $20 billion Source
Amazon agreed to make up to $20.0 billion available to Anthropic, released as AWS reaches delivery milestones for compute under their amended commercial agreement.

Draws are Anthropic convertible notes or, after an IPO, Anthropic shares. Amazon used $5.0 billion of it for Anthropic Series H stock, leaving $15.0 billion.

2 arrangements: Parent guarantee, Vendor financing Sources (4)
CoreWeave$15.5 billion Source (11)
CoreWeave, Inc. unconditionally guarantees all obligations of its special purpose borrowers under the DDTL 1.0, 2.0, 2.1 and 3.0 GPU facilities.

The first two were led by Blackstone and Magnetar; DDTL 3.0 has MUFG as agent. So these lenders hold both the GPU collateral and a claim on the parent.

4 arrangements: Contract lenders rely on, Lease guarantee, Parent guarantee Sources (11)
AMD$13.3 billion Source
AMD signed data center leases on its own credit that it expects to assign or sublease to commercial partners: aggregate future payments $13.3 billion over 10 to 15 years, commencing from the second quarter of fiscal 2027.

AMD remains the lessee if partners do not take them.

7 arrangements: Backstop, Credit support, Guarantee, Lease guarantee, Vendor financing, Warrant to a customer Sources
OpenAIup to $11.9 billion Source
CoreWeave's DDTL 3.0 facility of up to $2.6 billion is sized on, and secured by, OpenAI's March 2025 contract and its first order form.

OpenAI committed to pay CoreWeave up to about $11.9 billion through October 2030 under that agreement. The lenders, with MUFG as agent, therefore rely on OpenAI's payments.

Commitments total $3,645 million of bank loans and private notes held in a separate financing vehicle.

The supplier is protected by the parent before any customer financing is in place.

Some vested at the IPO; the rest vest on Milam County project financing or on SB Energy equity value thresholds. Fair value was about $4.603 billion at issuance and about $2.3 billion at 30 September 2026.

Is Nvidia a central bank?

Liquidity provision

Equity into buyers of Nvidia systems.

Partly supported Analysis

Investees pair Nvidia money with Nvidia compute; co-investors paid the same terms.

For

  • Nvidia bought $10.0 billion of stock in Anthropic, which rents Nvidia GPUs. Source (4)
  • Nscale took Nvidia equity and notes, relying on uncommitted financing. Source (3)

Against

  • Google bought identical Anthropic shares on the same terms. Source
  • Nvidia's Intel stake came with a product deal but no disclosed purchase commitment. Source (2)

Collateral support

Guaranties that make GPU debt bankable.

Partly supported Analysis

Borrowers and a landlord's noteholders cite Nvidia support; CoreWeave's lenders do not.

For

  • SB Energy says PORTS-Pike's financeability depends in significant part on Nvidia's guaranty; OpenAI is not investment grade. Source (3)
  • Galaxy's CoreWeave-tenanted notes cite Nvidia's capacity order and stake. Source (2)
  • Nvidia says it acted as customers outgrew their credit. Source (2)

Against

  • No CoreWeave credit agreement names the order. Source (3)
  • PORTS-Pike has no debt. Source
  • Google, Broadcom and AMD also backstop demand for their own chips. Source (4)

Pricing of money

Nvidia's entry sets borrowing costs.

Not testable Analysis

No source ties a round price or loan spread to Nvidia.

For

    Against

    • Others led: GIC and Coatue at Anthropic, ASML at Mistral. Source (2)

    Lender of last resort

    Nvidia rescues firms others will not fund.

    Not supported Analysis

    No rescue deal is sourced; two backed firms rely on uncommitted financing.

    For

    • SharonAI says it needs further financing; Nvidia pays minimum revenue on its unsold capacity. Source (2)

    Against

    • Nvidia can end the CoreWeave order after a 90 day insolvency. Source
    • Intel raised $23.0 billion of equity; Anthropic held $95.6 billion of cash. Source (2)

    Where the analogy breaks

    Nvidia cannot create money. Its guarantees reach a $118.0 billion maximum against $266.7 billion of shareholders' equity at 25 October 2026; the OpenAI guaranty alone is $105 billion, recoverable only from OpenAI. Its support depends on the same AI demand. Sources (5)

    Nvidia gives equity and credit support to its buyers from a finite balance sheet; price setting and rescue are not shown.

    Analysis The verdicts are judgments on the evidence shown, not facts reported by any company.

    How the data was gathered

    Every relationship starts from what Nvidia was legally required to disclose: its annual and quarterly reports, current reports, holdings reports and ownership filings since January 2023. Then the same deal was traced in what the other company filed: its annual and quarterly reports, prospectuses, credit agreements and indentures, newest first. Company releases fill deals that never reached a filing. A sweep of every company's filings for Nvidia near words such as backstop, guarantee, warrant and lease found the rest.

    Pages from the named news publications could not be read when this register was compiled, so almost every figure rests on filings and company releases. Reported figures that could not be read are listed as needing a quote and are not shown. The register holds 1,301 citations: 1,295 primary and 6 from news. 54 of 81 relationships are disclosed by one side only.

    Source policy

    A figure is shown only if a primary source (a filing, the company's own release, a regulator, a court, a lien registry or a rating agency's public release) or two independent named publications (Bloomberg, Reuters, The Wall Street Journal, the Financial Times, The Information, CNBC, Barron's, The Economist, Nikkei Asia, Axios) contain it. Otherwise it reads "Not confirmed". Blogs, social posts, aggregators and sell-side notes are never used. Every quote was found word for word in a saved copy of its source, and every number sits in or beside that quote.

    Definitions

    Funded
    Cash Nvidia has paid. On the page it counts the cost of shares still held: a stake partly sold counts only the part still reported.
    Committed
    A legally binding amount under a definitive agreement. Where no source says how much has been paid, it is counted once and never called unpaid.
    Contingent maximum
    The most Nvidia could be required to pay under a guarantee, backstop or similar promise, with the trigger stated. A guaranty that cannot yet be called is labeled not yet in force.
    Headline
    The largest figure announced, often "up to". Shown, never added to exposure.
    Gross exposure
    Funded plus committed plus contingent maximum, using confirmed amounts only. If any part is not disclosed it is a lower bound and reads "at least".
    Capacity backstop
    A promise to buy computing capacity that a cloud provider cannot sell to anyone else.
    Residual value guarantee
    A promise to cover the gap between an asset's guaranteed value and what it fetches when a lease ends or fails.
    Wrong-way risk
    Specific: Nvidia's exposure grows as the other company weakens. General: both move with AI demand. None: neither.
    Both sides
    Reconciled: both companies describe the deal the same way. Partly: they agree it exists but differ on terms. One side only: the other company has said nothing. Contradicted: they disagree on whether it exists or binds.
    Exposure at default
    Funded plus committed not yet paid plus the contingent maximum times a draw rate. The worst case draws everything; the base case is "not estimated" unless the draw is sourced. Loss is exposure less what Nvidia would receive or recover. Analysis

    Significance score

    score = 40 x gross exposure percentile + 25 x contingent share of gross + 15 x circularity percentile + 10 x counterparty weakness + 10 x lender reliance. Each part runs from 0 to 1. A part that cannot be computed scores 0.5, so an opaque private company is not ranked as the safest. Weakness comes from the indicators shown in each credit read, never from a letter grade. Analysis

    Staying current

    Watchers check Nvidia's filings every two hours on weekdays, every counterparty's filings every four hours, holdings and ownership filings daily, and named publications twice a day. Anything new goes to a review queue; nothing reaches this page until a person approves it. An amount of $1 billion or more, or any letter of intent, is re-verified every 30 days; other definitive deals every 90 days; completed or ended deals every year. Past its limit an amount shows "Not re-verified since" its date.

    Not investment advice

    This page describes financial exposure from public sources. It does not recommend buying or selling any security. Figures can be wrong or out of date; every one links to its source so you can check it.
